Bubble Sort (with early exit)
Insertion Sort and Selection Sort
Merge Sort
O(n log n) in every case / O(n) space
Quick Sort (Lomuto partition)
Average O(n log n), worst case O(n²) on already-sorted input with a last-element pivot. Use a random pivot to avoid that. It sorts in place.
Heap Sort (in place, O(n log n) worst case)

Build a max-heap bottom-up, then repeatedly swap the root to the end and shrink the heap. O(n log n) in every case and O(1) extra space, but not stable and cache-unfriendly, so quick sort is usually faster in practice. Introsort (C++ std::sort) falls back to heap sort when quick sort recursion gets too deep.
Counting Sort (small integer range)

No comparisons, so it beats the Ω(n log n) comparison bound: O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space, where k is the value range. Use it only when k is not much bigger than n. The prefix-sum + backwards pass keeps it stable, which radix sort depends on.
Radix Sort (LSD, non-negative integers)

Sort by the least significant digit first, using a stable counting sort each pass. O(d · (n + b)) for d digits in base b, effectively linear for fixed-width keys. Negatives need separate handling (or an offset). Bucket sort is the related idea for uniformly distributed floats: O(n) average.
Quick Sort with a random pivot and Hoare partition

A random pivot makes the O(n²) worst case (sorted input with a fixed pivot) extremely unlikely. Hoare does about three times fewer swaps than Lomuto and handles many duplicates better. For heavy duplicates, use 3-way partitioning (Dutch National Flag). Recursing into the smaller side first bounds the stack at O(log n).
Quickselect: Kth largest element in O(n) average

Like quick sort, but only continue into the side that contains the target index: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n) average, O(n²) worst. Compare with a size-k heap (O(n log k), better for streams) and full sorting (O(n log n)).
Count Inversions (pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]) using merge sort

When a right-half element is placed before remaining left-half elements, it forms an inversion with every one of them. O(n log n) instead of O(n²). It measures how "unsorted" an array is; the same trick solves "Reverse Pairs" and "Count of Smaller Numbers After Self".
Largest Number (sort with a custom comparator)

The order is defined by which concatenation is larger, not by numeric value ("3" before "30" because 330 > 303). A comparator must be consistent (transitive), which this one is. O(n log n · L). Related Java points: Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...), Integer.compare instead of subtraction (overflow), and the fact that Arrays.sort on objects is stable (TimSort).
Quick sort vs merge sort vs heap sort: which do you pick?

| Quick sort | Merge sort | Heap sort
Average time | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n)
Worst time | O(n²) (bad pivots) | O(n log n) | O(n log n)
Extra space | O(log n) stack | O(n) buffer | O(1)
Stable | No | Yes | No
In practice | Fastest on arrays (cache friendly) | Best for linked lists and external sorting | Slower constant factor, jumps around memory
Rule of thumb: quick sort (random pivot) for general in-memory arrays, merge sort when you need stability or are sorting a linked list or data that does not fit in memory, heap sort when you need a guaranteed O(n log n) with O(1) extra space.
Arrays.sort(int[]) vs Arrays.sort(Object[]) vs Collections.sort: why different algorithms?

| Arrays.sort(int[]) | Arrays.sort(T[]) / List.sort
Algorithm | Dual-pivot quicksort | TimSort (merge + insertion)
Stable | Not needed (equal ints are identical) | Yes, guaranteed
Worst case | O(n log n) since JDK 14 (falls back to heap sort) | O(n log n)
Nearly sorted input | No special gain | Close to O(n): it finds existing runs
Extra memory | O(log n) | Up to n/2 references
Interview tip: stability only matters when equal keys are distinguishable, which is why objects get a stable sort and primitives do not. Collections.sort(list) just calls list.sort(null), which uses the object array sort.
Comparison sorts vs counting sort vs radix sort: when can you beat O(n log n)?

| Comparison sort | Counting sort | Radix sort (LSD)
Time | O(n log n) lower bound | O(n + k), k = value range | O(d · (n + b)), d digits, base b
Space | O(1) to O(n) | O(k) counts (+ O(n) output) | O(n + b)
Works on | Anything with a Comparator | Small integer ranges | Integers, fixed-length strings
Stable | Depends | Yes (with prefix sums) | Yes, and it must be: each pass relies on the previous one
Breaks when | Rarely | Range is huge (ages fine, phone numbers not) | Keys are long or not digit-based
Rule of thumb: the O(n log n) bound only applies to sorts that compare elements. If keys are small integers (ages, scores 0–100, letters), counting sort is O(n); for wider fixed-width integers use radix sort.
Kth largest element: full sort vs min-heap of size k vs quickselect

| Sort, then index | Min-heap of size k | Quickselect
Time | O(n log n) | O(n log k) | O(n) average, O(n²) worst
Extra space | O(1) to O(n) | O(k) | O(1) (in place)
Modifies input | Yes (or copy) | No | Yes, reorders it
Streaming data | No | Yes, one element at a time | No, needs the whole array
Code to write | 2 lines | 5 lines | Partition + loop, easy to get wrong
Interview tip: say the sort answer first, then offer the heap (safe, works on a stream) and mention quickselect with a random pivot as the O(n) average option.
Lomuto vs Hoare partition: what is the practical difference?

| Lomuto | Hoare
Pointers | Two moving the same way (i, j) | Two moving toward each other
Swaps | More (about 3× Hoare on average) | Fewer
Pivot ends up | At its final index, returned | Not necessarily at the split point
Recursion split | (lo, p-1) and (p+1, hi) | (lo, p) and (p+1, hi)
All-equal input | O(n²): everything lands on one side | Splits evenly
Rule of thumb: Lomuto is easier to write correctly on a whiteboard and is what quickselect usually uses; Hoare is faster and handles duplicates better. Mixing up the recursion bounds between the two is the most common bug.
